emails.preview: The signal was public the whole time. Nobody was reading it. So I built a tool that does.
emails.body_plain:
Welcome. First, the thing people ask me up front: I'm not a VC, and I'm not competing with you for deals. GitDealFlow is a tool. It watches 350+ startups' public GitHub engineering activity and flags the ones quietly heating up — in your sectors — before they're raising or in the press.

You don't read code. You don't crunch anything. It surfaces them. You just look.

Here's why I built it, because it starts with a mistake I kept making.

I was watching a small fintech startup from my laptop in Athens. Nothing special on the surface. No press. No AngelList buzz. No warm intros circulating. But their GitHub told a different story.

In two weeks, their engineering output tripled. Four new contributors joined. They spun up three new infrastructure repos. They were clearly shipping faster — all in public, for anyone to see.

I flagged it in my notes. Three weeks later, they announced a $4M Series A led by a top-tier fund.

The investors who got in had seen something I missed. Or maybe they just knew someone. Either way, the signal was right there in plain sight the whole time. Public. Free. Updating in real time.

Nobody was reading it.

So I built a tool that does. Every Sunday, I'll send you the five startups heating up early — shipping faster, pulling in new contributors, standing up new infrastructure. The kind of early engineering signal that tends to show up 21 to 47 days before fundraises hit the press.

Tomorrow, I want to challenge something you probably believe about your current deal flow.

emails.subject: From a laptop in Athens: how I stumbled onto the signal
emails.preview: No partner network. No demo-day badge. Just one nerd reading GitHub. Here's what happened.
emails.body_plain:
I'm The Data Nerd. That's the name I use because the methodology should carry the argument — not my face, not my background, not a LinkedIn selfie.

For ten years I wrote small angel cheques out of Athens, not San Francisco. No partner network. No demo-day badge. I'd rather read a commit history than work a conference.

So I heard about the good companies the same way you do: a week too late, after the round was full and the price had jumped. That part actually stung.

Then in 2024 I watched a small fintech team — three founders, one repo, no press, no warm intros circulating. Two weeks later their engineers were suddenly shipping far more: commit activity tripled, new contributors piled in, new infrastructure appeared out of nowhere.

Three weeks after that, a $4M Series A led by a top-tier fund. Every clue had been sitting in the open on GitHub the whole time. I couldn't un-see it.

So I built a tool that reads that trail across 350+ startups every week and hands me the names quietly taking off — in plain words, no code. Now I send those names to you.

And yes — I'm just one nerd reading GitHub. That's the point: no committee, no spin, no agenda. The read is fully automated, it ships on a schedule, and the whole method is published on SSRN with an open dataset.

What it watches: which teams are suddenly building a lot more.
What you get: a name, what it does, and a simple reason it's taking off.
What you do: reach out early, while it's still quiet.

Next email: the one finding that changed everything — and it's not what you think.

emails.subject: The 3.4x finding that changed how I read startups
emails.preview: Velocity matters. But the shape of the velocity matters more. Here's the data.
emails.body_plain:
Here's the finding that made me stop and rebuild the whole model.

I had been ranking startups by commit velocity alone. More commits = hotter startup. Simple. But when I backtested 219 confirmed fundraises against the signal, the correlation was decent — not great. Some startups with high velocity raised nothing. Some with modest velocity raised big rounds.

The missing piece was contributor concentration.

A startup where one developer does 80% of the commits can spike just as hard as a team where eight developers are sharing the load. But only one of those teams looks like a fundraise candidate to a Series A partner.

So I combined two metrics: 14-day commit velocity acceleration AND contributor diversity, measured by the Gini coefficient over the same window. A Gini coefficient under 0.30 means the work is spread across multiple contributors — a real team, not a solo founder in a crunch.

Startups that meet both conditions — high acceleration AND low contributor concentration — are 3.4× more likely to announce a Series A within 60 days than startups with high acceleration alone.

3.4×. That's not noise. That's a signal you can build a sourcing strategy around.

The full methodology is published as an SSRN preprint (abstract=6606558), with the panel of all 219 backtested fundraises, the regression stratified by stage, and the open dataset. You can check every call yourself — I'd rather you verify than believe.
